articles.title: Trouble beneath the waves: India’s submarine fleet is ageing and replacements are years away
articles.summary: The Navy’s conventional submarine fleet is ageing at a time when the need for new undersea vessels is growing.
articles.body: The Navy’s conventional submarine fleet is ageing at a time when the need for new undersea vessels is growing. Yet plans to replace and expand this critical arm of the Navy remain years away from delivery, raising concerns about a widening gap in underwater combat capabilities.The Navy currently operates 16 conventional diesel-electric submarines across three classes (Kalvari, Sindhughosh and Shishumar) alongside three strategic submarines.Its plan to induct 24 conventional submarines by 2030 has fallen behind schedule. Four Sindhughosh-class boats have been retired, including INS Sindhughosh, the lead vessel of the class, while only six Kalvari-class Scorpene submarines have been inducted. The Shishumar-class boats have undergone mid-life upgrades, but average around 35 years in age, and capability gaps remain. With more older submarines due to be retired in the coming years, the pressure to replenish the fleet is mounting.A 30-year submarine-building plan drawn up in 1998 by Vice Admiral AK Chatterji envisaged parallel foreign and domestic construction programmes, with the aim of building up the fleet by 2030. That ambition, however, has fallen well behind schedule.India’s strategic submarine programme has progressed faster. INS Aridaman, the third Arihant-class ballistic missile submarine, has strengthened the country’s nuclear triad, alongside land-based missiles and aircraft. It is designed to carry up to eight K-4 nuclear-capable missiles, each with a range of 3,500 km. A fourth ballistic missile submarine has been launched at Visakhapatnam, while the larger S-5 class is planned for the future.Submarines are the hardest leg of the nuclear triad to track because they can remain concealed deep underwater. This makes them crucial to a credible nuclear deterrent, allowing a country to retain the ability to retaliate even if its land-based assets come under attack.Their value extends beyond nuclear deterrence. Earlier this year, a US submarine reportedly tracked and sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena off Sri Lanka without the warship detecting the underwater threat. The episode highlighted the advantage submarines can have over surface vessels when operating undetected.For conventional submarines, one of the most important technologies is air-independent propulsion (AIP), which allows them to remain submerged for two to three weeks without surfacing or snorkelling to recharge their batteries. Boats without AIP must snorkel more frequently, increasing their vulnerability to detection by aircraft and surface vessels. Only the six Kalvari-class submarines are slated to receive a DRDO-developed AIP system.The most significant procurement effort is Project 75I, a tender worth around Rs 70,000 crore for six to nine submarines. Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders and Germany’s Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) have cleared the technical evaluation stage, with India moving towards final cost negotiations for at least six Type 214 submarines equipped with AIP. However, deliveries will take years, with the first submarine expected about seven years after the contract is signed.India is also looking to expand domestic manufacturing of submarine weapons. Hyderabad-based VEM Technologies has signed an agreement with TKMS to manufacture heavyweight torpedoes in the country.Project 76, an indigenous conventional submarine programme, is expected to follow, with the proposed submarine family incorporating a modified DRDO-developed AIP system.The Navy also plans to develop nuclear-powered attack submarines under Project 77. The Cabinet Committee on Security has approved two such submarines, worth Rs 35,000 crore, with the first expected by 2036-37.The Navy also plans to lease a nuclear-powered attack submarine from Russia to strengthen its capabilities in the interim.The Navy expects to acquire at least 22 domestically built submarines under these programmes.

articles.title: Sally Rooney’s characters ask questions. Her politics only has rigid answers.
articles.summary: “Life is the thing you bring with you inside your own head.” ― Sally Rooney, Normal People In the quiet, emotionally-fraught spaces of Irish author Sally
articles.body: “Life is the thing you bring with you inside your own head.”― Sally Rooney, Normal PeopleIn the quiet, emotionally-fraught spaces of Irish author Sally Rooney’s novels, young people sit in cramped Dublin flats, scroll through instant messages, and struggle to bridge the terrifying distance between what they feel and what they are able to say. This core philosophy—a distinct trait of young people everywhere, especially Gen Z—is what made Rooney get the moniker of “voice of this generation”.Connell and Marianne, the protagonists of Normal People, are at their most vulnerable when they have the most to say to each other yet cannot find the words. They are intelligent and highly educated. They are also acutely conscious of social hierarchies that shape their lives. Yet they repeatedly misinterpret each other’s deepest needs. They possess profound psychological insight into one another, yet they consistently fail each other in ways that seem almost inexplicable. One gets to see this as a reader, and marvel at it because it mimics our real lives so much.What made Conell and Marianne’s relationship so affecting to millions around the world is that Rooney does not offer either character the comfort of being entirely right. They are capable of both tenderness and cruelty – often within the span of a single conversation. It feels so familiar, isn’t it?That’s the power of Rooney. She established her reputation writing about people who are far more articulate than they are certain – quite telling of our times. Her characters can fluently dissect late capitalism and structural inequality, but they struggle to understand their own relationships. They think, argue, retreat, contradict themselves, and hurt the people they love.What made Rooney such a compelling chronicler of her generation was her understanding that having the right opinions did not necessarily make anyone a better human being. Yet this internal narrative nuance stands in stark contrast to the uncompromising political stances taken by Rooney in her public life.The tension between the novelist who embraces the ambiguity of human nature; and the public figure who insists on absolute moral commitments has created one of the most intriguing cultural conundrums of the times we live in.The art of intimate uncertaintyRooney’s fiction operates on a fundamental truth: political correctness does not grant emotional immunity. In her debut novel, Conversations with Friends, the protagonist Frances, and her friend Bobbi, navigate complex romantic entanglements while maintaining a veneer of radical left-wing sophistication.Bobbi identifies as a communitarian anarchist, while Frances’s mother is a social democrat. They debate global geopolitics, class privilege, and structural oppression over dinner tables, yet their private actions are routinely marked by emotional cowardice, deceit, and moral carelessness.For instance, Frances reflects in Conversations with Friends that political theory often functions as an analytical shield against personal vulnerability: “Things and people moved around me, taking positions in obscure hierarchies, participating in systems I didn't know about and never would... You live through certain things before you understand them. You can’t always take the analytical position,” says she.In Normal People, class dynamics press heavily upon Connell and Marianne, but these structural forces do not dictate a straightforward moral narrative. When the two characters discuss the economic inequities of Trinity College or the absurdity of capitalist markets, their shared political consensus does not save them from hurting one another.Rooney perfectly captures the tragedy of young intellectuals who understand the systemic roots of world problems but remain helpless to fix their own emotional lives.This thematic inquiry deepens in Beautiful World, Where Are You with long, philosophical email exchanges between Alice, a successful novelist, and Eileen, an underpaid editorial assistant. They obsess over global civilizational collapse, climate catastrophe, and political futility.Yet, amidst these macro-level anxieties, their primary concerns remain interpersonal: who loves whom, who replied to a text message, and how to find happiness in a fragile world. Eileen encapsulates this paradox in an email to Alice: “Maybe we’re just born to love and worry about the people we know, and to go on loving and worrying even when there are more important things we should be doing.”Across her novels, Rooney portrays human relationships as messy, non-linear, and resistant to dogmatic formulas. Her characters ask open-ended questions about how to live ethically under broken economic systems, but the stories themselves refuse to supply simple, moralizing answers.The Paradox: Inner vulnerability vs. outer righteousnessIn her public life, however, Rooney abandons the nuanced doubt of her fiction in favour of an uncompromising political posture. While her fiction is celebrated for its soft, probing exploration of human error, her real-world political identity is defined by absolute clarity and an unwillingness to tolerate dissent or ambiguity.This contrast became starkly evident in October 2026, when Rooney agreed to withdraw her entire book catalog from sale in the United Kingdom (UK) following her public pledge to donate book royalties to Palestine Action.There is a profound distinction between critiquing right-wing policies or opposing war and actively pledging financial backing to a radical direct-action group (that was officially proscribed as a terrorist organization by the British government under anti-terrorism legislation). Under British law, remitting earnings to a proscribed group carries severe criminal liabilities.When her publisher, Faber, clarified that continuing to supply her books in the UK had become legally impossible without committing a crime, Rooney accepted the total commercial removal of her works—including Normal People, which had sold over one million copies in the UK market alone. She also canceled public appearances in the UK, citing the threat of arrest.This action forces a critical question: How does an author whose creative work is devoted to understanding human vulnerability end up embracing a political framework so absolute that it leaves no room for legal, social, or moral gray areas?Herd mentality, moral aggrandizing, and the ideological trapRooney’s real-world stance offers a case study in the socio-psychological tensions of contemporary cultural elites. Her trajectory highlights several defining psychological dynamics of our cultural moment, like the paradox of fighting totalitarianism with absolute dogma. The irony is not lost here.In modern political discourse, activism often adopts the very traits it claims to oppose. In attempting to resist injustice or authoritarian policies, activists frequently drift into binary, uncompromising mindsets.Rooney’s real-world posture mirrors this dynamic: while her fiction critiques the suffocating nature of rigid social systems, her political statements exhibit an unyielding and totalizing moral certainty. It raises a troubling psychological question: Why do intellectuals who champion human empathy in their art so easily adopt rigid, black-and-white dogmas in their politics?Moral aggrandizing and performative certaintyIn the age of social media and elite ideological bubbles, holding radical political views has become a form of social currency. ‘Moral aggrandizing’—the impulse to demonstrate personal moral superiority through extreme political purity—drives public figures to take ever more rigid stands to prove their dedication.In her fiction, Rooney brilliantly satirizes characters who use progressive jargon to cover up their selfish behaviour. As Bobbi tells Frances in Conversations with Friends: “You underestimate your own power so you don’t have to blame yourself for treating other people badly. You tell yourself stories about it.”Yet in her public life, Rooney appears susceptible to the very trap her characters fall into: prioritizing an ideological gesture over the complex realities of dialogue, nuance, and engagement.The strange world of cultural elitesWhy do contemporary literary figures so often line up behind identical political stances? Is it because modern cultural landscape incentivizes groupthink? Where dissenting from the orthodoxy of one’s social or artistic peer group carries heavy personal and professional costs?While Rooney’s public actions are framed as radical defiance against state authority, they simultaneously align with the ideological expectations of her elite literary community. The desire to remain morally pure within one's tribe often outweighs the willingness to engage with the messy, uncomfortable compromises of real-world politics.The novelist vs. the dogmatistSally Rooney is not the first writer to embody this conflict between the open-ended empathy of literature and the rigid certainty of public ideology. Literary history is filled with authors whose creative works embraced human ambiguity while their personal lives were defined by unyielding doctrine.Milan Kundera and the trap of the ‘agelast’: Czech novelist Milan Kundera devoted his essay collection The Art of the Novel to exploring the threat that political dogma poses to creative literature. Kundera argued that the novel is the domain of the “wisdom of uncertainty”—a space where no one owns the absolute truth and where human actions are treated as open questions.Kundera borrowed the term agelast (Greek)—meaning “one who does not laugh” or lacks humour—to describe ideological zealots who believe the truth is self-evident and that everyone must agree with them. He warned that dogmatists cannot tolerate literature because fiction insists on ambiguity, whereas ideology demands absolute obedience.Rooney’s novels belong firmly to the Kunderan tradition of doubt, yet her public political persona risks morphing into the very agelast Kundera warned against — an ideologue who demands absolute, non-negotiable moral alignment.Leo Tolstoy: The compassionate novelist vs. the moral zealot: Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy provides another historical parallel. In War and Peace and Anna Karenina, Tolstoy showed an astonishing capacity to empathize with deeply flawed human beings. His characters make disastrous mistakes, harbour contradictory motives, and wander in spiritual darkness, yet Tolstoy treats them with profound narrative grace.In his later life, unfortunately, Tolstoy underwent a radical shift. He embraced a rigid, uncompromising form of Christian anarchism, denounced his own literary masterpieces as immoral, and issued severe, black-and-white moral decrees to his followers.Rooney’s choice to allow her books to be withdrawn from UK bookstores brings her underlying paradox into sharp focus. It leaves readers and critics with fundamental questions about art, psychology, and public life in our era.The questions that stand out are:Why do modern intellectuals create art that celebrates human imperfection while adopting public stances that tolerate no imperfection at all? Has political activism in the cultural sphere become less about achieving practical outcomes and more about demonstrating moral purity?When an author insists on binary answers in the real world, does it inevitably undermine the open-ended empathy that makes her fiction so moving?Rooney’s fictional characters—Connell, Marianne, Frances, and Alice—are fascinating because they are flawed, uncertain, and are constantly asking how to love and live in a confusing world. They remind us that human beings are rarely as clean or consistent as their political theories.Yet as long as the author holds firmly to uncompromising positions in her public life, the tension will remain between the novelist who explores the uncertainties and contradictions of being human and the public figure who appears unwilling to make room for doubt.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Wikipedia’s editorial safeguards failed to correct antisemitic content, ADL says
articles.summary: ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt says 91% of a banned Wikipedia editor's biased edits on Israel, Hamas and October 7 pages remain live and unchecked.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: More than a year after the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) uncovered a group of at least 30 Wikipedia editors seemingly coordinating to add anti-Israel bias, misleading information and antisemitic narratives, the group says the online encyclopedia has yet to edit or remove much of the concerning content. "We had expected that these editors would be removed. We had expected that their edits would have been reversed. We expected that new policies would have implemented. Almost nothing has changed," ADL CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. In the 2025 report, "Editing for Hate," the ADL raised several issues, including a "coordinated campaign" of manipulation of Wikipedia content related to Israel, Palestine and similar topics. Additionally, the organization said it found pro-Hamas perspectives informing Arabic-language content on those same topics. The group of 30 editors, according to the ADL, were more active than comparable groups "by a factor of at least two." WIKIPEDIA CO-FOUNDER SAYS LEFT'S 'RELENTLESS' TAKEOVER OF MASS MEDIA RUINED THE WEBSITE HE HELPED BUILD Wikipedia's community banned some of the editors from the topic area or from the site entirely following the 2025 report. However, the ADL claims the issues that it flagged were not resolved with the restrictions on those named in its previous report. In its 2026 report, "Damage Done: Wikipedia Leaves Biased Edits Unchecked Despite Editor Bans," the ADL stated that "no banned editor's body of work has been systemically reviewed to determine which edits should be corrected." The organization found that across seven articles reviewed for its 2026 report, six of which are "flagship pages," 91% of a banned editor's edits were still live. "A topic ban is great in theory, but in practice, if you're not doing it, if you aren't really taking action, there's really no ban at all," Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. "It's as if you had an individual who was spraying graffiti on the walls of public buildings. You might arrest that individual, but you don't erase or clean up the graffiti. You still leave it on the public institutions. Like, no one would do that in the real world. I don't know why that is acceptable as a practice on Wikipedia." An account known as Iskandar323, which was part of the group of 30 editors documented in the 2025 report, serves as a case study of what has happened in the time since then. The ADL found that the account had a years-long editing history that showed a notable uptick following Hamas' Oct. 7 attacks in Israel. The account, according to the ADL, made 485 edits across six articles, 225 of which came after the Hamas massacre, including 85 that were made in Oct. 2023. The ADL noted that the six pages that were edited "are among the highest-trafficked English-language Wikipedia entries on the topic." The pages were "Israel," "Gaza war," "October 7 attacks," "Hamas," "Zionism" and "Jews." NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK Wikipedia's Arbitration Committee (ArbCom) discussed Iskandar323's conduct in public proceedings. ArbCom found that Iskandar323 "engaged in disruptive behavior in the PIA topic area, including consistently non-neutral editing." The account was given a site ban after continuing to edit topics related to Israel and Palestine despite already being under a topic ban, according to the ADL. Just days after the Oct. 7 attacks, Iskandar323 removed much of the substance of Wikipedia's "Hamas" article, including materials detailing the group's antisemitism, anti-Zionism, use of human shields and child combatants, human rights abuses and more to "a far less-read companion article" titled "Criticism of Hamas." The ADL said that Iskandar323 left only a "brief generalized reference behind." The organization noted that while nothing had been deleted, the moving of information made it so readers viewing the "Hamas" page would no longer see the material unless they went to a subsequent page. On Nov. 21, 2023, the same account removed around 17,000 characters of text and citations from Wikipedia's "Gaza war" page, according to the ADL. The account deleted a section of the page detailing forensic evidence of violence committed during the Oct. 7 attacks, including decapitation, torture and sexual violence. Two days later, Iskandar323 removed around 7,400 characters from what remained on the page, including witness accounts from Israeli soldiers and ZAKA, a first-responder organization. "These are not innocuous edits," Greenblatt said. "These are intentional changes designed to drive a narrative, a narrative that number one, demonizes the Jewish state. That, number two, removes all context from terror incidents in general, and specifically, specifically, that sanitizes and launders what happened on October the 7th, the worst, most brutal attack on the Jewish people since the Holocaust." The ADL said that the consequences of the biased edits go beyond Wikipedia itself, calling the platform "the foundational infrastructure for the broader online ecosystem." Wikipedia is often favored by search engines, and can be "at or near the top of search results for most substantive queries," according to the ADL. Greenblatt said that "Wikipedia has lost trust" at a crucial time as many large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and AI features embedded into other products rely on Wikipedia. ALARMING STUDY FINDS TOP CHATBOTS MORE LIKELY TO REPEAT FALSEHOODS FROM THE LEFT: ‘TRULY ASTONISHING’ Pressure from congressional scrutiny, federal inquiries and Wikipedia's own enforcement following the 2025 report appeared to lead to a significant decrease in coordinated activity among the 30-editor group, according to the ADL. However, the organization acknowledges that while "visible signs of coordination" decreased, it does not necessarily mean that it has stopped. The 2026 report states that the problematic edits are still happening, but through "quieter, subtler techniques." A July 2026 review identified 19 active accounts that have been editing articles related to Israel and Palestine, according to the ADL. The organization said that eight of the editors had avoided sanctions despite being part of the original 30 identified in the 2025 report. These editors are allegedly using subtle techniques, such as undoing other editors' changes, hedging factual claims and rebuilding articles slowly to avoid detection. The other 11 editors have histories with Wikipedia, despite being new to the ADL's documentation. Like those in the group identified by the ADL over a year ago, the records of these editors — some of whom have been editing the site for years — are mostly on articles related to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Across the 229 articles where the 19 accounts overlapped, the ADL found that the 11 newly identified editors were "far more active recently" and held the most recent edit on roughly six in 10 pages. "I think the public has come to really appreciate that Wikipedia is, in theory, this source of unbiased information, has kind of integrity to it," Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. "But when Wikipedia is poisoning the public conversation because it is enforcing the intolerance encoded in it by these editors, it's pushing the prejudiced agenda of these anonymous actors, it's no longer an unbiased source of information. It's become, actually, a weapon." Ultimately, the ADL gave a series of recommendations aimed at the Wikimedia Foundation, policymakers, search engines and AI developers, as well as the press and the public. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The ADL called on the Wikimedia Foundation to strengthen accountability on sensitive pages by privately verifying editors' identities, ending anonymous IP-address editing and requiring vetted editors to resolve disputes. It also urged the Wikimedia Foundation to establish a task force on antisemitic bias modeled after the foundation's 2021 intervention against Holocaust revisionism. For search engines and AI developers, the ADL is asking for more transparency when relying on Wikipedia as a source for an answer, particularly on sensitive topics. The organization also encouraged them to consider editorial caveats based on the topic, update information and develop bias-detection benchmarks. When it comes to policymakers, the ADL would like to see continued oversight hearings on bias and antisemitism on Wikipedia, the creation of a task force to monitor coordinated content manipulation and the development of policy options by academics, technologists, Wikipedians and civil society leaders. The ADL is also calling on the press and the public to recognize that chatbots and AI search summaries may be relying on Wikipedia's framing, even without disclosing that. It also urges individuals and the media to verify citations and quotes on AI-generated answers. articles.title: IMD announces onset of northeast monsoon; Tamil Nadu likely to get normal rainfall
articles.summary: CHENNAI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) announced the onset of the northeast monsoon over south peninsular India on Thursday, forecasting
articles.body: CHENNAI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) announced the onset of the northeast monsoon over south peninsular India on Thursday, forecasting normal rainfall for Tamil Nadu overall, with regional variations.V R Durai, director, Area Cyclone Warning Centre, Regional Meteorological Centre, Chennai, said northern districts might receive below-normal rainfall, while southern districts might get normal to above-normal rainfall. Coastal districts are expected to receive normal rainfall.Tamil Nadu receives an average 45cm rainfall during the northeast monsoon, around 48% of the annual rainfall. Chennai receives 87cm, around 60% of the annual rainfall.Daytime temperatures may remain above normal under the influence of El Niño, the IMD official said.Durai said Tamil Nadu recorded a 21% rainfall deficit during the June-September southwest monsoon season, making 2026 the state’s third most deficient year since 2006.
